Response from an admin:

There are definitely still plenty of issues, but it's also not nearly as bad as it used to be. If you think the server issues haven't improved since 2010, I don't think you really remember what it was like. Back then, the site was completely down for hours at a time quite regularly. It wasn't uncommon at all for it to be totally inaccessible for half a day once a week or so. Now you have to refresh multiple times to get some pages to load, but the site's almost never actually down any more.

As for the continuing issues, I'd say it's mostly a combination of lack of resources devoted to improving the situation, and the general difficulties that come from the way the site has grown and its current scale. reddit's never really had more than 2 sysadmins at a time, and most of the time they're busy with just keeping things running (while also doing various other jobs like being "the IT guy", because there's nobody else) so they can't really devote much time to trying to improve the weak points. There also aren't usually more than 1 or 2 developers actively trying to work on infrastructure-type stuff, and even when they are working on it (they have other responsibilities as well), it's not always possible to tell if what they're doing will end up improving things much in the end. Part of this is because of the scale of reddit and the sheer amount of data constantly coming in with new posts and voting.

To give a specific example, very large comment threads are definitely a major issue. When there's a really big thread like a game thread for the superbowl or an incredibly popular AMA, it can seriously impact the entire site. This problem has existed for years[1] . So quite a while ago (and a little before I started working here, so the details might not be completely accurate), a developer devoted a lot of time to doing a complete rewrite of the way that we store comment threads to try to fix these issues. He spent a long time on it, and when it was finally deployed... it ran into previously unknown issues in Cassandra (one of our data-storage systems) that nobody had ever seen before, because nobody else had ever tried to use certain features in it at this volume/scale. The people that maintain Cassandra haven't been able to figure out the issue, so we've had a complete comment-tree rewrite for years that should, in theory, fix the issues with large threads, but we can't use it.

Keep in mind as well that reddit's traffic is also constantly growing at a fairly high rate, so things only get harder. Years ago when Obama did his AMA, the amount of traffic it brought in was completely unprecedented, and basically destroyed the site. Now our traffic is significantly above that level at pretty much all times (maybe all the time, I haven't been following traffic numbers much lately). It's not easy to keep up with, and honestly I think reddit does a pretty amazing job at being able to handle the amount of traffic it does with as few people as it has. I don't think there are any other sites nearly this large with such a small team. We definitely know there are still lots of server issues, we see the error pages just as often as you do.
I remember the bad old days of downtime back in the late aughts. Things certainly have improved since then.

it's a compelling enough idea. a well-implemented system of player-created content is often enough to extend the lifespan of games for years and years. but people are mistaken if they think that this will bring the tabletop D&D experience to a software environment. the biggest strength of pen and paper RPG systems is that you can break whatever rules you want. you can create unique artifacts, spells, creatures, cities, and entire WORLDS, and then roleplay out what happens within that space. what i see here is a dungeon crawler that, instead of being randomly/procedurally generated, has a person on the other end instead. all the trailer really shows is combat. if it's just going to be another quest-giver-hack-and-slash, i'll probably give it a pass.

I agree with you on the whole but I think it will serve as a way for people who have never been a part of the hobby to kind of test the waters. Nothing can ever replace that weekly 4-6 hour session though!

Not just for the DMs, but also the players, I've observed a DM happily plop an Adamantine Golem in front of a party, only for one player to simply turn the floor under it into mud, have the golem fall through it and then through every single level of the tower below, hitting the ground floor and going deep enough that it could not get out. DM was sad... Time and again players will resort to the most abstract non-combat solutions to get through situations, which is simply too many variables to anticipate.

I don't see that quite happening in a setting where humans need to code the setting, but then again, what people lose in plasticity people might gain in ease. This won't be a replacement, not until we can hook the brain up the generate stuff directly could computers replace what tabletop does to an equal degree.
